sources.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
sources.locator: §§11-12, PDF pp. 86-100 of the 107-page author PDF: the discrete Fourier transform and the fast Fourier transform, read in full in the PDF text.

contents.name: §11 opening: the finite cyclic group Γ_n = ⟨ω⟩, ω = e^{2πi/n}; the pairing (ω^j, ℓ) ↦ ω^{jℓ}; the discrete transforms f# (11.1) and ĝ (11.2)
§11 Proposition 11.1 and (11.4): Φ_n: L²(Γ_n) → L²(Z_n) is a unitary isomorphism, with the inverse transform of (11.2) and the inversion formula
§11 formula (11.5): the L² conventions, counting measure on Z_n and (1/n)·counting measure on Γ_n
§11 (11.6) and Proposition 11.2: the functions e_j(ω^k) = ω^{jk} form an orthonormal basis, proved by the geometric-sum orthogonality computation with the case ω^m = 1 separated
§11 Proposition 11.3: the aliasing identity f#(ℓ) = Σ_{j∈Z} f̂(ℓ+jn) for absolutely convergent Fourier series on S¹
contents.reason: The discretisation aliasing identity is the continuous-to-lattice interface used by the sampling page (FR-19), which owns periodisation and Poisson summation; FR-18 proves only exact finite identities.

contents.name: §11 Propositions 11.3-11.4 and the discretisation operators R_n, E_n and the multiplier comparison (11.20)-(11.29), including the centered-difference second-order estimate
contents.reason: Numerical discretisation-error estimates for Fourier series on the circle; no FR-18 row approximates continuous functions and the page proves exact finite identities only.

contents.name: §11 (11.30)-(11.31): discrete convolution and Fourier multipliers on Γ_n, F(D_n)u = (k_F ∗ u)
§11 (11.32)-(11.33): the discrete Poisson kernel p_y(ω^j) written as a sum of two finite geometric series, with the closed form
contents.reason: Closed-form summation of the discrete heat/Poisson kernel; the finite transform page needs only the general convolution identity, and no FR-18 row evaluates that kernel.

contents.name: §11 Proposition 11.5, (11.34)-(11.40), and exercises 1-8: Gauss sums, their evaluation by the Gaussian integral, and the quadratic-reciprocity applications
contents.reason: Number-theoretic Gauss-sum evaluations and quadratic reciprocity; they sit on the number-theory track and no FR-18 row uses them.

contents.name: §12 (12.1)-(12.3): the direct computation count (n² multiplications, n(n-1) additions of complex numbers) and the Γ_4 identities
§12 (12.4)-(12.7): the explicit Γ_4 decomposition 2f#(2ℓ) = 0f#(ℓ), 2f#(2ℓ+1) = 1f#(ℓ)
§12 (12.8)-(12.11) and Proposition 12.1: the input-half functions 0f, 1f and the identities n f#(2ℓ) = 0f#(ℓ), n f#(2ℓ+1) = 1f#(ℓ) (decimation in frequency)
§12 cost paragraph after (12.13): after k iterations, kn additions and kn/2 complex multiplications, plus the comparable integer operations and memory fetches
§12 (12.14)-(12.23) and the following discussion: the iterative implementation, bit reversal, the in-place variant, and machine-dependent trade-offs
contents.reason: Implementation engineering (array variants, bit reversal, in-place updates, machine-dependent optimisation); FR-18 specifies the recursive algorithm and proves correctness and the arithmetic-operation count, not an implementation.

contents.name: §12 exercises 1-3: program the recursion, apply it to the heat equation, and discuss multidimensional transforms and memory
contents.reason: Programming and application exercises with no theorem consumed by FR-18.

contents.name: §12 exercise 4: generalisation of the FFT algorithm to n = 3^k and to products of small primes

sources.title: MIT 18.310 lecture 23, The Finite Fourier Transform and the Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm (course page)
sources.locator: Complete unpaginated lecture, headings 1-4 (Introduction; The Fourier Transform; The Finite Fourier Transform; The Cooley-Tukey Fast Fourier Transform Algorithm), read in full from the course HTML.

contents.name: Heading 1: Fourier series, orthogonality of sines, and the coefficient formula
Heading 2: the Fourier transform as an integral representation and the eigenfunction motivation
Heading 3: the finite Fourier transform as evaluation of a degree n-1 polynomial at the n roots of unity, with a primitive n-th root, and the symmetric forward form Σ_j a_j z^{jk}
Heading 3: the inverse transformation by multiplying each p_k by z^{-sk} and summing, giving a_s = (1/n)Σ_k p_k z^{-sk} via the power sums of the roots
Heading 3: the direct n² evaluation/coefficient-recovery cost of the naive method
Heading 4: the Cooley-Tukey reduction for n = 2s: 2s evaluations reduce to two s-point transforms after s additions, s subtractions and s multiplications
Heading 4: iteration of the reduction until degree 0, producing the evaluations
Heading 4: the worked example on coefficients (1,3,2,5) modulo 17 with 4 a primitive fourth root, and the inverse division by n

sources.title: Manfred Einsiedler and Thomas Ward, Ergodic Theory with a View Towards Number Theory, Appendix C (course-hosted full text)
sources.locator: Appendix C.1-C.3, printed pp. 429-439: topological groups and Haar measure (C.1-C.2), character groups with the compact-open topology, orthogonality of characters, Parseval (C.3 through Theorem C.10 and Example C.14), read in the full text.

contents.name: C.1 Definition C.1, Lemma C.2, Example C.3: topological groups, compactness and metrisability, GL_n(C)
C.2: Haar measure on locally compact groups; Examples C.5, including counting measure on a discrete group and the multiplicative measure |z|^{-1}dx on C∖{0}
C.3: characters as continuous homomorphisms into S¹, the dual group Ĝ with pointwise multiplication and the compact-open topology, and Theorem C.6 (the dual is LCA; separating subgroups are dense)
C.3: the Fourier transform on L¹(G), its separating self-adjoint algebra of images, the convolution law, and the L¹ → L∞ bound; Lemma C.7 (discrete groups have compact duals and conversely)
C.3 following Lemma C.7: the orthogonality computation ∫_G (χη^{-1})(g) dm_G = 0 for distinct characters, and the derivative fact that the trivial character is isolated in Ĝ
C.3 Theorem C.8: the Parseval formula ⟨f,g⟩_G = ⟨f̂, ĝ⟩_Ĝ for L² functions on an LCA group
C.3 Theorem C.9 (Herglotz-Bochner) and Theorem C.10 (inversion for L¹ ∩ B(G), with the compact-group normalisation of counting measure on the dual)
contents.reason: Bochner's theorem and the LCA inversion theorem with its measure normalisation are the subject of the FR-16 supplier page (in-run batch 26); FR-18 uses only the finite-dimensional case proved directly on this page.

contents.name: C.3 Theorem C.11 and the following completeness discussion: for compact abelian G the characters form a complete orthonormal basis, proved by Stone-Weierstrass
contents.reason: Completeness of the character system for general compact abelian groups; the finite case here is finite-dimensional and needs no Stone-Weierstrass argument.

contents.name: C.3 Theorem C.12 (Pontryagin duality), Theorem C.13 (annihilator and quotient duals), dual homomorphisms, and the torsion/monothetic discussion
contents.reason: Pontryagin duality and the annihilator calculus are the subject of the FR-17 supplier page (in-run batch 27); FR-18 cites only the published finite cyclic instance for its character family.

contents.name: C.3 Example C.14: computed duals of Z, R, locally compact fields K, and Q_p, plus the solenoid remark for discrete Q
C.3 Example C.14(2) and (3): the duals of R and of locally compact non-discrete fields
C.3 Lemma C.15 (Riemann-Lebesgue for absolutely continuous measures) and Lemma C.16 (the measure-theoretic refinement on S¹)
contents.reason: Riemann-Lebesgue on LCA groups is scaffolded on the FR-16 supplier page (batch 26, thm-riemann-lebesgue-lemma-on-lca-groups); Lemma C.16 is a measure-theoretic refinement not used by FR-18.

contents.name: Heading 3: the forward evaluations p(z^k), the inverse a_s = (1/n)Σ p_k z^{-sk}, and the degenerate small lengths
Heading 3: the transform converts polynomial products into pointwise products
Heading 3: recovering coefficients from values requires the length to cover the polynomial degree; otherwise the reduction modulo z^n-1 wraps coefficients
Heading 4: the reduction is stated for n even (n = 2s) and iterated to powers of two
Heading 4: the worked four-coefficient computation, executed in two levels
